paragraphs: Alexey Fyodorovitch Karamazov was the third son of Fyodor Pavlovitch Karamazov, a landowner well known in our district in his own day. He is still remembered among us because of his gloomy and tragic death, which happened thirteen years ago and which I will describe in its proper place. For now I will only say that this “landowner”—for so we used to call him, although he hardly spent a day of his life on his own estate—was a strange type, but one fairly often met with: abject and vicious, and at the same time senseless. But he was one of those senseless people who are perfectly able to look after their worldly affairs and, apparently, nothing else. Fyodor Pavlovitch, for instance, began with next to nothing. His estate was of the smallest. He ran to dine at other men’s tables and fastened on them as a toady. Yet at his death it turned out that he had a hundred thousand roubles in hard cash. All the same, he was all his life one of the most senseless, fantastical fellows in the whole district. I repeat, it was not stupidity—most of these fantastical fellows are shrewd and intelligent enough—but just senselessness, and a peculiarly national form of it.

He was married twice and had three sons: the eldest, Dmitri, by his first wife, and two, Ivan and Alexey, by his second. Fyodor Pavlovitch’s first wife, Adelaïda Ivanovna, came from a fairly rich and distinguished noble family, also landowners in our district, the Miüsovs. How an heiress, who was also a beauty—and moreover one of those vigorous, intelligent girls so common in this generation, though sometimes found in the last as well—could marry such a worthless, puny weakling (as we all called him), I won’t try to explain. I knew a young lady of the last “romantic” generation who, after some years of a mysterious passion for a gentleman she could easily have married at any moment, invented insurmountable obstacles to their union. She ended by throwing herself one stormy night from a high bank, almost a precipice, into a rather deep and fast river, and so died, entirely to satisfy her own caprice and to be like Shakespeare’s Ophelia. Indeed, if this precipice, a place she had chosen and loved, had been less picturesque, if there had been a prosaic flat bank there instead, most likely the suicide would never have happened. This is a fact, and probably there have been quite a few similar cases in the last two or three generations. Adelaïda Ivanovna Miüsov’s action was no doubt likewise an echo of other people’s ideas, and came from the irritation of living without mental freedom. She wanted, perhaps, to show her feminine independence, to defy class distinctions and the despotism of her family. And a pliable imagination persuaded her, we must suppose, for a brief moment, that Fyodor Pavlovitch, in spite of his parasitic position, was one of the bold and ironical spirits of that progressive age, though he was in fact an ill-natured buffoon and nothing more. What gave the marriage its piquancy was that it was preceded by an elopement, and this greatly captivated Adelaïda Ivanovna’s fancy. Fyodor Pavlovitch’s position at the time made him especially eager for any such venture, for he was passionately anxious to make a career one way or another. To attach himself to a good family and get a dowry was an alluring prospect. As for mutual love, it apparently did not exist, either in the bride or in him, in spite of Adelaïda Ivanovna’s beauty. This was perhaps a unique case in the life of Fyodor Pavlovitch, who was always of a voluptuous temper and ready to run after any petticoat at the slightest encouragement. She seems to have been the only woman who made no particular appeal to his senses.

Right after the elopement Adelaïda Ivanovna realized in a flash that she felt nothing for her husband but contempt. So the marriage showed its true colors with extraordinary speed. The family accepted the event fairly quickly and gave the runaway bride her dowry. But the husband and wife began to lead a thoroughly disorderly life, and there were endless scenes between them. It was said that the young wife showed incomparably more generosity and dignity than Fyodor Pavlovitch. As is now known, he got hold of all her money, up to twenty-five thousand roubles, as soon as she received it, so that those thousands were lost to her for ever. He did his utmost for a long time to get the little village and the rather fine town house that formed part of her dowry transferred to his name by some deed of conveyance. He would probably have succeeded, simply from her moral exhaustion and her wish to be rid of him, and from the contempt and loathing he aroused by his persistent and shameless pestering. But, fortunately, Adelaïda Ivanovna’s family stepped in and thwarted his greed. It is known for a fact that the husband and wife often came to blows, but rumor had it that Fyodor Pavlovitch did not beat his wife but was beaten by her, for she was a hot-tempered, bold, dark-browed, impatient woman with remarkable physical strength. In the end she left the house and ran away from Fyodor Pavlovitch with a penniless divinity student, leaving Mitya, a child of three, in her husband’s hands. Fyodor Pavlovitch immediately set up a regular harem in the house and gave himself over to drunken orgies. In the intervals he would drive all over the province, tearfully complaining to everyone that Adelaïda Ivanovna had left him. He went into details too disgraceful for a husband to mention about his own married life. What seemed to please him most and flatter his self-love was to play the ridiculous part of the injured husband and parade his woes with embellishments.

“One would think you’d been promoted, Fyodor Pavlovitch, you seem so pleased in spite of your sorrow,” scoffers said to him. Many even added that he was glad of a new comic part to play the buffoon in, and that he pretended not to notice his ludicrous position simply to make it funnier. But who knows, it may have been simplicity. At last he succeeded in getting on the track of his runaway wife. The poor woman turned out to be in Petersburg, where she had gone with her divinity student and thrown herself into a life of complete emancipation. Fyodor Pavlovitch at once began bustling about, getting ready to go to Petersburg, with what object he could not himself have said. He might really have gone. But having decided to go, he felt at once entitled to fortify himself for the journey with another bout of reckless drinking. And just at that time his wife’s family received news of her death in Petersburg. She had died quite suddenly in a garret, of typhus according to one story, or of starvation according to another. Fyodor Pavlovitch was drunk when he heard of his wife’s death. The story is that he ran out into the street and began shouting with joy, raising his hands to Heaven: “Lord, now You let Your servant depart in peace.” Others say he wept without restraint like a little child, so much so that people were sorry for him, in spite of the repulsion he inspired. It is quite possible that both versions were true: that he rejoiced at his release and at the same time wept for her who released him. As a general rule, people, even the wicked, are much more naïve and simple-hearted than we suppose. And we ourselves are, too.
